items.content:
Your post died at 500 impressions again.

(LinkedIn's engineers explained why)

I've spent 5 months studying 3+ technical documents LinkedIn published on the new algorithm: the engineering blog, the retrieval paper, and their VP of Engineering's feed breakdown.

Reach jail is a real mechanism. So is the way out.

LinkedIn's A/B tests showed +3.29% revenue and +1.17% more professional interactions for members with fewer connections. The rebuild favors small accounts. You just have to give it something to work with.

How you get in:

→ You're posting to the wrong room.

Your followers are old colleagues, peers, and connections from 2019. They follow you. They don't buy from you. They're the audience your content gets judged by first. When they shrug, it never travels past them.

→ Buyers never see it.

Your post lives in two places: your connections' feeds by default, and a suggested content pool where the system matches it to strangers by meaning. Both run from minute one. And both can fail. A vague post gives the system nothing to match. A shrugging network gives it no confidence signal, so the wider push never comes.

→ Reach jail.

The system converts engagement into percentile buckets: "71st percentile" instead of raw view counts. Flop with the wrong first audience and you sit in a low bucket the model won't push wider. Embeddings update within 30 minutes, so the burial happens fast.

How you get out:

→ Fix the profile first.

Five author fields travel with every post: your name, headline, company, industry, and title. Your headline is telling the algorithm what you're qualified to talk about before anyone reads a word.

→ Post growth + authority.

The suggested content system retrieves 2,000 candidates from hundreds of millions, and it matches on meaning. Growth content is how you enter that pool: hot takes, trends. Its job is reach: strangers finding you. Authority content is what those strangers find when they click your profile: frameworks, client results, how you actually run things. Its job is trust.

→ Go where your buyers are.

A sharp comment on a post with 50K impressions puts your name in front of every buyer reading it, and the good ones click your profile. Reciprocity is real: the people you show up for show up for your posts, and their engagement lifts your percentile out of jail.

→ Build the relationship.

Connect, DM, coffee chat. The algorithm decides who sees your post. It can't follow up with the CMO who read your case study and said nothing. That part is still manual. It's the part that compounds: posts have a lifespan of days, relationships keep paying out quarters later.

→ Pull them off-platform.

LinkedIn rents you the audience and can change the terms whenever it wants. Your newsletter is the part you own.

Save this for the next time a post flatlines and you want to blame the algorithm.

PS: I built a free audit kit from this research. 8 rules, AI prompts, checklists etc → https://lnkd.in/ewrc93QS

items.content:
One of the misconceptions about procurement is that it's all about negotiating prices 💷 .
.
.
.
I understand why people think that. After all, procurement professionals spend a great deal of time working with suppliers. But over the years I've learnt that focusing on suppliers too early can mean overlooking the real opportunity.

I remember visiting a manufacturing business that wanted help reducing purchasing costs. Before I arrived, the owner had already assembled files containing supplier quotations, contracts and price histories. He expected we'd spend the day comparing costs. Instead, I asked if we could take a walk around the factory first.

We spent the morning talking to people rather than looking at paperwork. We watched materials arrive, followed jobs through production and listened carefully to the conversations taking place between departments.
Just before lunch the owner looked at me and said, "I thought we were here to talk about suppliers." The truth was that we already were. 

Every delay in production affects purchasing decisions. Every inaccurate stock record influences replenishment. Every unclear production schedule creates unnecessary urgency or lack of action.

None of those issues began with the supplier, yet they all eventually land on the purchasing team's desk.

Strong procurement doesn't necessarily begin with buying. It begins with understanding how the whole business works together. Only then can purchasing become the strategic function it was always intended to be.

Some of the largest commercial improvements I've helped businesses achieve, came not from negotiating harder, but from helping different parts of the business work together more effectively.

items.content:
Its the small things that slowly empty the bucket.
.
.
.
People sometimes ask me where I normally find the biggest opportunities to improve a manufacturing business.

It's an interesting question because, after more than four decades in industry, the answer is almost never what people expect.

Many imagine I arrive with a checklist of supplier costs to reduce or contracts to renegotiate. Those things certainly have their place, but they rarely tell the whole story. More often than not, the clues appear long before I've looked at a single purchase order.

I remember walking around a factory with a Managing Director who was understandably proud of what he'd built. The order book was healthy, the machines were busy and there was an obvious sense of commitment from the people working there. If you'd driven past the building, you would probably have assumed everything was running exactly as it should.

As we talked, I noticed a forklift driver making the same journey backwards and forwards between two departments. Nobody seemed particularly concerned because it had become part of the daily routine. A little later, I watched a supervisor leave a production meeting because someone needed a decision that only he could make. Then an operator stopped work for a few minutes while waiting for clarification about the next job.

None of those moments lasted very long and none of them would have appeared on the monthly management report but they all had something in common: They represented tiny interruptions that had quietly become accepted as normal.

That's the thing about manufacturing businesses. They rarely lose significant profit because of one catastrophic mistake. More often, profit disappears through hundreds of perfectly ordinary habits that nobody has questioned for years.

When you've worked in the same business every day, it's remarkably easy to stop seeing what is right in front of you. We all do it. Familiarity has a way of disguising inefficiency.

That is one of the reasons I enjoy carrying out Business Performance Reviews. The most rewarding moment isn't producing the report. It's the owner's reaction when they suddenly notice something they've walked past every day for years.

Those moments often become the beginning of meaningful change.

From my own experience, one lesson my career has taught me is that factories rarely need heroes. They need systems that make it easier for good people to do good work. Once those systems improve, profitability usually follows.

items.content:
Looking at your business through someone else's eyes 👀.
.
.
.
"If you bought your own business tomorrow, what would frustrate you first?"

I've asked that question of several Managing Directors and almost every time the response is the same. There's a pause, followed by a smile 🙂 , and then a thoughtful conversation.

I remember one owner beginning the factory tour with enormous pride, and rightly so. He'd spent years building the business from the ground up. He knew every customer by name, every supplier, every machine and every member of staff.

Towards the end of the tour, I asked him that question. He looked at me for a moment before saying, "I've never thought about it like that."

What followed wasn't criticism of his business. Quite the opposite. It was a fascinating discussion about all the little compromises that had accumulated over the years. Processes that only existed in people's memories. Supplier agreements that had simply rolled on from one year to the next. Reports that nobody entirely trusted but everyone continued producing because they'd always done so.

There was nothing unusual about any of it, in fact, that's precisely why it interests me. Businesses evolve, they adapt, they respond to customers, markets and opportunities. Along the way they also collect habits, workarounds and assumptions that eventually become invisible or frustrating to the people closest to them.

Stepping back and looking at your own business as though you were a potential buyer 💷 , can be an unexpectedly revealing exercise.

Sometimes the greatest opportunity isn't changing the business, it's simply seeing it differently 👓.

From my own experience, whether I've been working in quality management, procurement or operations, I've found that asking thoughtful questions ❓ nearly always reveals more than arriving with ready-made answers.

items.content:
Cyber-attacks 💻 are becoming frighteningly common place, and this is getting corporate buyers understandably twitchy. 

No buyer wants to declare to their business that production may be affected if / when their supplier gets hacked. So, what cyber-security credentials do SME Manufacturers need to prove to their customers buyers to stay in the supply chain?
.
.
.
Now, please note that I am not cyber security expert, but whilst I was working for a client, I needed to spend some time talking with IT professionals and insurance companies after some big brand names were effectively closed down for a period of time. 

During this process I learned a few things that you may wish to consider:

1.	Ensure your IT asset register 📒 is up to date: Most failed supplier assessments begin with poor knowledge of what kit and systems exist, what version software they have installed, who uses them and what data they hold.
2.	Be clear on where your buyer-sensitive data is held 🔏 : this demonstrates you have control and clarity over commercially sensitive information. This is especially important where you as an SME handles customer drawings, prototypes, schedules, financial data or personal data.
3.	Create a “Supplier Cyber Evidence pack” 📦 : In here you need to have the latest records of policies, training records, an incident action plan, insurance policy documents etc.
4.	Implement the five “Cyber Essential” control areas: this consists of evidence covering firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection and patch management. If you have a third-party IT provider, I recommend you verify they have all of this in hand.
5.	Enable Multi Factor Authentication 📲 : this can be a challenge when some business data and systems are accessible on staff personal phones. I had quite a difficulty finding a solution when some didn’t want to lock their own phone!
6.	Train your staff and retain the records 📜 : there are many online courses now that have a test at the end and create a certificate and a training record.
7.	Consider cyber insurance: this is not necessarily a cheap option but the cover and peace of mind, in case of business interruption, is a relief. I must say that the insurance broker I selected was extremely helpful and supportive here.

There are many more actions to consider but I’m sure you get the idea. 

If you really want to get serious, take a look at ISO 27001 certification for example, the standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS). 

Also talk to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and IASME. They are very helpful. 

It can be surprising what procurement / operational professionals get involved in.

When manufacturing businesses are working harder than ever 🥵 , why in many does cash 💷 remain tight?
.
.
.
Growth is great but when not managed effectively it often creates:
·       Higher stock levels 📈 
·       Increased debtor days 😢 
·       Greater work in progress 
·       More operational complexity

A business can be profitable on paper and still struggle financially. That is why smart owners pay close attention to:
·       Inventory levels and churn by product
·       Purchasing practices and contracts
·       Commodity and currency price fluctuations 📉 
·       Customer payment terms and their adherence to them 
·       Production efficiency, waste generation and effective recycling 🌳 

Cash flow problems often start long before they appear in the bank account, and the warning signs are usually hiding in the operation. 

·       Do you have the right key measures in place and are you actively tracking them?
·       Is your business strategy and direction clear to all employees and are they following it?
·       Are your team clear on their responsibilities and are they holding themselves and each other to account?
·       Do you have the right players in your team and are they getting the best out of their people and each other?
·       Are you proud of your work environment and are pleased to showcase it whenever a customer arrives, even when unexpected?
·       Are your processes, policies, systems simple, documented and followed by all?

If you are unable to tick ✅ each of these positively and sincerely you may need support. Fast track your business without spending hours, days and weeks learning, testing and talking about it.

items.content:
Many SME Manufacturing and Engineering companies are feeling acute pain 🤕 . Some are asking:- "How can we renegotiate commercial terms with our suppliers and customers before our margins disappear?"
.
.
.
I get it, it is not easy. You are being squeezed from all angles, but there are actions that you can take. 

Here are a few suggestions from my playbook:

1.	Establish where you are achieving margin and where not: Many companies do not drill into their data and know what money they are earning by product and customer. If you don’t know its time to get your finance person on the case. Not all customers are the same. Some may be more open to and capable of absorbing price increases than others. Do you know who are which?

2.	Stop 🛑  uncontrolled and unnecessary discounting: Some discounts are given away too easily and often become a quick way of trying to win orders however they can have a massive impact on your margins and profitability. 

3.	Check your supply and customer contracts 🗒️ : Look at sections regarding price variation, MOQ’s, delivery terms, payment terms, force majeure etc. What wiggle room is there, or not? Don’t take anything for granted.

4.	Challenge price increases 🫸 : Not all price increase requests are reasonable and supported by evidence. Have you asked for the evidence, have you checked their facts, can they effectively demonstrate every penny of the price increase, are you checking against published indices, are their competitors doing the same, what is happening to your competitors? Unfortunately, some suppliers seize any opportunity to over inflate their increase.

5.	Are other terms of business an option rather than price ❓ : In negotiations price is not always the most important factor. Maybe it’s the payment term? Are other trade-offs possible that would be better for your business?

6.	Make price increases temporary ⏱️ : Don’t accept an increase without considering their reversal when markets/commodities/currencies adjust back in the future.

These are but a few of the options available. 

What money 💷 are you leaving on the table or giving away? 

Is your purchasing function delivering 🚚  and safeguarding 🦸 your bottom line?

Why do Sales purposely create barriers between themselves and their customers?
.
.
.
I recently decided to switch mobile network provider. Not because of cost but due to a poor signal in the area I had moved too.

Speaking to a new provider was easy and the experience positive but when seeking subsequent technical support – what a nightmare !

Why is it that you are presented with a myriad of “Options” when you ring, but they often do not include one you want? 

Why can there not be an option of “Speak to a person if none of the above are appropriate?”

I received my new SIM in the post, but it stated a different mobile to that I am transferring and the blurb enclosed did not mention this. So, I called my future network provider to clarify next steps, but could I find an option to speak to a human being? 

Eventually I decided to choose the “Thinking of leaving us? option” and not surprisingly I was put through to a person.

The person was great and everything sorted so I asked “It is now Saturday, at what time will I be able to changeover to the new SIM? 
Stupidly I expected this to be the same day or perhaps the next. Nope ! 
That will be WEDNESDAY sir because it is a bank holiday weekend. 

What? 

In this world of technology and AI, why does it take 5 days to switch mobile provider after having received and activated my new SIM?

Two more things. 
1.       Do the people who actually set up these automated response systems actually have people trial and test them, then act on the feedback?
2.       Why in this digital age can providers take your money instantly but not provide the service just as quickly?

I read that insertable SIM’s may be a thing of the past soon and a digital solution is on its way. I certainly hope so.

Changing supplier, if not done carefully, can cause huge disruption, a drain on resources and massive failure in the supply chain. The outcome must be worth the investment 📈 . Just measuring the purchase price is incomplete, the total cost to change must be calculated, measured and monitored.

items.content:
One question that is being asked is; how do we cost effectively change to a ‘Just In Case’ stock model to improve supply to our customers, as material and product supplies are so unreliable, erratic and costly?
.
.
.
The answer is that you are not.

The good news 🌞  is that there are many actions that can be taken to try and address this difficult situation many are facing right now. I will mention a few actions you could do now, but I have many thoughts on addressing this conundrum.

1.	Stop panic buying 🛒 : A reaction is often to buy more right now because we don’t know when there will be more available. ‘Toilet paper’ is all I say on this! Do your due diligence and homework. Some businesses use the strategy to sell more by creating panic to suit their own agenda.

2.	Carefully analyse your stock data 📋 : What parts or materials are the showstoppers and what is their current stock position and availability, even if at a higher price.

3.	Call your premium customers 🌟 : If you are not getting a regular forecast, it may be sensible to speak to those customers that you rate highest, determine their current situation and expectations for more product.

4.	Turn old stock into cash 💷 : Many businesses have a fair chunk of materials etc that have gathered dust for some time. Some of this stock has a real cash value. Perhaps those that you purchased it from originally may love to buy it back for another customer they have. It may be sensible to turn this dusty old stuff into cash and use that to buy stock you really need.

5.	Look at your supply contracts 🔎 : It may be both in your interest and that of your supplier to have a stocking agreement or call off arrangement. Don’t ask, don’t get. Don’t make assumptions. Sometimes suppliers will ringfence certain stock for you and not charge if you do not take it. It may be a regular standard item that they can sell easily to someone else.

6.	Re-assess your safety stock levels 📦 : I have seen safety stocks that were appropriate years ago still enforced. The situation is changing all of the time so it is surprising how irregularly stocking parameters are left static and unchecked.

These are just a few suggestions. 

Is your business doing the above? 

As a business owner, are you running the numbers 🏃‍➡️ or hoping that someone on your team is doing it 🙏 ?

Purchasing and Supply Chain professionals should be doing this and much more as their day job. If you cannot afford to employ one, how are you bridging 🌉 the gap?
